Merryhearted
MER-ee-har-ted
adj. (glad of heart; in Isaiah 24, the last people to stop singing when the earth is judged)
English merry + heart. At Isaiah 24:7 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning the glad of heart — the naturally cheerful, whose sighing marks how deep the judgment has gone.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 24 is the chapter sometimes called the prophet's apocalypse, a judgment not on one nation but on the earth, and it measures the disaster by the silence: The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh. Then: The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth. The prophet does not count the dead. He counts the instruments that have stopped. And the surest sign that the thing has reached bottom is that the merryhearted are sighing — the people who could always find a reason to sing have run out.

Scripture treats a glad heart as a real good, not a lesser spiritual state. A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance; a merry heart doeth good like a medicine; and the feasts of Israel were commanded celebrations with wine and music in them. So when Isaiah wants to say that a judgment is total he takes the gladness away, and when he wants to say that the story does not end there he puts it back — the same chapter closes with the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously, and two chapters later the mountain is covered with a feast of fat things. The mirth of tabrets ceases; the joy of the LORD does not, and the book knows the difference between the two.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): having a merry heart; gay of disposition; cheerful in temper.

expand to see more

MERRYHEARTED, a. Having a merry heart; cheerful; gay.

MIRTH, n. Social merriment; hilarity; gaiety with laughter.

TABRET, n. A tabor; a small drum used as an accompaniment to a pipe or fife.

LANGUISH, v.i. To lose strength or animation; to pine; to droop; to fade.

SIGH, n. A single deep respiration; a long breath; the inspiration of a larger quantity of air than usual.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 24:7 — "The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh."

Isaiah 24:8 — "The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth."

Isaiah 24:11 — "There is a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone."

Isaiah 24:23 — "Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously."

Modern Corruption

Christian gladness is confused with the mirth Isaiah says will cease, so that believers either chase the one or suspect the other, when Scripture distinguishes them plainly.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors have made a mess of Christian joy. The first identifies it with the mirth of Isaiah 24 — a mood produced by wine, music and good circumstances — and so manufactures it in the meeting with lighting and volume, with the result that when the circumstances turn, the joy turns with them. The second, reacting, suspects gladness altogether, and produces congregations where laughter feels out of place. Scripture holds both ends: it commands feasts, says a merry heart doeth good like a medicine, and also says the mirth of the land is gone when God judges.

The difference is the source, and Isaiah 24 makes it visible by taking one away and leaving the other. The tabrets stop; the reign of the LORD of hosts in mount Zion does not. Nehemiah gives the positive form of the same thing to a congregation weeping over the law: the joy of the LORD is your strength — a gladness whose ground is outside the hearer and therefore survives the vintage failing. A Christian who has only the first kind of joy will be merryhearted until the wine mourns; a Christian who has the second will sigh honestly with Isaiah and still have something left.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew simchath leb (H8056 / H3820), glad of heart; toph (H8596), a tabret; anach (H584), to sigh or groan.

expand to see more

Hebrew sameach lev (H8056, H3820) — merry of heart; the phrase the AV compounds into one word.

Hebrew anach (H584) — to sigh, to groan; what the merryhearted are reduced to.

Hebrew toph (H8596) — a tabret, a hand drum; the first instrument to fall silent.

Hebrew masos (H4885) — exultation, mirth; the gladness of the land that is gone.

Hebrew amal (H535) — to languish, to droop; the state of the vine.

Usage

"“all the merryhearted do sigh” — the judgment measured by who has stopped singing."

"“The mirth of tabrets ceaseth” — the instruments counted rather than the dead."

"“the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion” — what does not cease."
